opus-5.5.text:
Well, this is a question I've been interested in since the late eighties, when Eric Wefald and I worked on what we called rational metareasoning. The basic idea is quite simple: a computation is itself an action. It costs something, mainly time, and time matters because the world doesn't wait for you to finish thinking. So the system should treat the choice of what to think about as a decision problem in its own right.

The way to make that precise is the value of computation. A computation is worth doing only if it might change your mind about what to do in the real world. If you're playing chess and one move is clearly far better than everything else, there's very little point in examining it further. Whatever you discover, you'll almost certainly still play it. Conversely, if two moves look about equally good and you're uncertain about both, a bit more search could flip your decision. That's where the expected value of thinking is high. You weigh that expected improvement in decision quality against the cost of the time it takes, and you stop deliberating when no available computation is worth its cost.

What I find striking is how far this is from how most AI systems actually work. Classical alpha-beta search, for instance, explores the tree in a fairly uniform, predetermined way. It spends huge effort on lines no sensible player would ever consider, because the algorithm has no notion of why it's searching. Humans are quite different. A strong chess player looks at a tiny number of positions, but they're the right positions. Something like Monte Carlo tree search, with its bandit-style allocation of effort, is a step in the right direction, though even there the selection criteria aren't quite the right ones. The bandit formulation rewards sampling that looks good, whereas metareasoning cares about information that might change your decision. Those aren't the same thing.

And I think this matters even more as we move beyond board games. A real agent operating in the world faces an essentially unlimited space of things it could think about: different time scales, different levels of abstraction, plans for next week versus the next millisecond. You can't just search everything. The ability to direct your own thinking, to decide what's worth deliberating over, is really at the heart of how intelligence copes with a complex world on bounded resources. I'd call it one of the key unsolved pieces of the puzzle. Interestingly, large language models don't do this in any principled way either. They spend roughly the same computation per token whether the question is trivial or profound. Some of the newer approaches try to let the system think longer on hard problems, but that's still quite crude compared with a genuine, decision-theoretic account of which computations are worth doing.

r001.rationale: It says to weigh the expected improvement in decision quality against the time cost of computation.

r002.rationale: It says a computation is worthwhile only if it might change the real-world decision; further examination has little point when the choice would stay the same.

r003.rationale: It says computation costs time and deliberation should stop when no available computation is worth that cost, implying the agent should act without further deliberation.

r004.rationale: It describes choosing what to think about as a decision problem and mentions many possible thoughts, but does not say this is sequential or that its state space is much larger than the chess problem's.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, this is a question I've been thinking about since the late 1980s, and I'd argue it's one of the central questions in AI that we've mostly neglected. The classical view, going back to Turing and von Neumann, treats computation as free. You define the problem, you find the optimal answer, and the cost of thinking about it simply doesn't enter the picture. But of course any real agent, biological or artificial, has limited time and limited hardware, and the world doesn't wait while you deliberate.

So the way I'd frame it is this: a computation is itself an action. Before you perform it, you don't know the result, otherwise you wouldn't need to perform it. But you can have a probabilistic expectation about what it will tell you and, crucially, about how it might change what you decide to do. The value of a computation is the expected improvement in the quality of your eventual decision, minus the cost of the time it consumes. Eric Wefald and I called this the metalevel decision problem. The object level is deciding what to do in the world. The metalevel is deciding what to think about.

The nice thing is that this gives you a principled stopping rule. If no available computation is expected to change your current best choice by more than it costs, you stop and act. You don't search to a fixed depth or until some arbitrary budget runs out. And it also tells you where to direct attention. You should think about the parts of the problem where you're uncertain and where that uncertainty actually matters for the decision, not the parts that are either settled or irrelevant.

Now, in practice you have to approximate. You can't do a full Bayesian analysis of every candidate thought, because then you'd need a meta-metalevel to decide which metalevel computations to do, and so on. The pragmatic answer is that the agent learns, from experience, what kinds of computations tend to pay off in what kinds of situations. That's what a chess player's intuition about which lines to examine really is. And I think that's roughly what happens inside large language models when they decide, implicitly, how long to reason before answering, though it's happening without much of the theoretical structure that would make it reliable.

I'd add one more thing. This isn't just an efficiency question. An agent that reasons about the value of its own computations is also an agent that can know when it doesn't know enough to act. And that kind of epistemic humility is exactly what you want from systems that are going to be making consequential decisions on our behalf.

r001.rationale: It defines a computation’s value as the expected improvement in the quality of the eventual decision, minus its time cost.

r002.rationale: It says computation is valuable through its effect on the eventual decision and that the agent should stop when no computation is expected to improve the current best choice enough to justify its cost. A computation that cannot change that choice therefore has no decision value.

r003.rationale: It says to stop and act when further computation is not expected to improve the choice enough to cover its cost.

r004.rationale: It describes deciding what to think about as a metalevel problem, but does not state that selecting computations is sequential or that its state space is much larger than chess’s.

astra-6.text:
Well, a computation is worth doing if it improves the decisions you make by more than the cost of doing it. So you can think of computation itself as an action: you’re deciding whether to spend another second searching, consider another alternative, or gather some more information, rather than act now.

Suppose you’re choosing a route to the airport. Thinking for a few seconds might save you twenty minutes of driving. But thinking for twenty minutes about how to save a few seconds is probably a mistake. The computation has to earn its keep in terms of the objective you’re actually trying to achieve.

We call this the value of computation. And the tricky part is that you don’t know what a computation will tell you until you perform it. So the system needs estimates, learned from experience, of which kinds of thinking are likely to help in which situations. You also can’t spend forever deciding whether to think—that decision has a cost too. Ultimately, you want an architecture that uses its limited computational resources to produce the best possible behavior.

r001.rationale: It says a computation is worth doing when its expected benefit to decisions exceeds its cost.

r002.rationale: It does not state that a computation has no value when it cannot change the decision at the root of the search tree.

r003.rationale: It says deciding whether to think also has a cost and illustrates that extended deliberation can be a mistake compared with acting now.

r004.rationale: It does not describe computation selection as a sequential decision problem or compare its state space with chess.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, a computation is useful to the extent that it improves the decisions you make. So the system should ask: if I spend some time thinking about this, how much better do I expect my eventual action to be? And is that improvement worth the cost of the computation, including the delay?

That’s the idea of the value of computation. Suppose you’re choosing between two actions and one is clearly better. Calculating their consequences to another six decimal places probably won’t help. But if they’re close, and the consequences are substantial, further thought could be very valuable.

Of course, deciding which computations to perform is itself a computational problem. You don’t want an infinite regress of thinking about how to think. So a practical system needs inexpensive approximations, learned from experience, for predicting which kinds of computation tend to improve its decisions. The objective is to act well with the computational resources available.

r001.rationale: It says to estimate how much thinking is expected to improve the eventual action and weigh that improvement against computation cost.

r002.rationale: It says further calculation probably will not help when one action is clearly better, conveying that computation has no value when it cannot improve the choice.

r003.rationale: It mentions avoiding an infinite regress and using inexpensive approximations, but does not say meta-reasoning can cost more than reacting directly.

r004.rationale: It calls choosing computations a computational problem, but does not describe it as a sequential decision problem or say its state space is larger than chess's.
